html:
About 1204 Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Turkic officer of the Ghurid sultans, seized western Bengal from the Sena kings. It brought Muslim rule to the eastern end of the Ganges plain within a dozen years of the Second Battle of Tarain.

Bakhtiyar was a soldier of fortune who had been turned down for service in Delhi. From a small land grant near Varanasi he raided Bihar, and about 1200 he stormed the Buddhist monastery of Odantapuri, killing the monks; he is said to have taken it for a fort. The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila is laid to his troops (see the decline of Buddhism).

He then rode on Nadia, a Sena capital. The chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj says he arrived with only eighteen horsemen, was taken for a horse trader, and broke into the palace while the old king Lakshmana Sena was at dinner. The king fled east by boat.

Bakhtiyar made his capital at Lakhnauti. In 1206 he marched toward Tibet, lost his army in the hills of Assam and was murdered by one of his own officers. His conquest lasted: Bengal was ruled by governors of the Delhi Sultanate and then by the independent Bengal Sultanate.
sum: About 1204 Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Turkic officer of the Ghurid sultans, seized western Bengal from the Sena kings. It brought Muslim rule to the eastern end of the Ganges plain within a dozen years of the Second Battle of Tarain.
